blocks.text: A desktop 3D printer moves its print head to within a fraction of a millimetre with no position sensor at all, while a robot arm lifting varying loads cannot afford to trust a motor to simply obey. The difference is the choice between a stepper motor that counts steps open-loop and a servo that measures and corrects its own position.

blocks.markdown: A **stepper motor** turns in discrete, repeatable increments. Each pulse sent to the driver advances the shaft by one **step angle** $\theta_s$. Common motors have 200 full steps per revolution ($\theta_s=1.8^\circ$). Positioning is **open-loop**: the controller counts pulses and assumes the rotor followed. A **servo** system adds a position sensor (an encoder or potentiometer) and compares the measured position with the command, driving the motor to reduce the error. This is **closed-loop** control.

blocks.title: Step angle and steps for a rotation
blocks.text: Step angle $\theta_s=360^\circ/N_{rev}$ where $N_{rev}$ is steps per revolution. With **microstepping** by a factor $m$ (the driver splits each full step into $m$ current levels), the effective step is $\theta_s/m$. The number of steps for a rotation $\Delta\theta$ is $n=\Delta\theta/(\theta_s/m)$.

blocks.caption: Step angle, steps for a rotation, and the pulse frequency needed for a given shaft speed in rev/s

blocks.title: Counting steps
blocks.prompt: A 1.8 degree stepper is driven in half-step mode (m = 2). How many pulses rotate the shaft by 135 degrees, and how many pulses per second give 10 rev/s?

steps.text: Pulse rate for 10 rev/s: $200\times2=400$ pulses per revolution.

blocks.answer: 150 pulses rotate the shaft 135 degrees; 4000 pulses/s gives 10 rev/s (600 rpm).

blocks.markdown: **Why open-loop works, and when it does not.** A stepper holds position because the rotor locks onto the magnetic field of the energised windings. As long as the load torque stays below the motor's **pull-out torque** at the commanded speed, every pulse produces exactly one step. If the torque or acceleration demand is exceeded the rotor **skips steps**, and because there is no feedback the controller never knows. A servo motor can use its full torque and speed range because the feedback corrects any error, but it needs a sensor, a controller and tuning.

rows: Printers, indexing tables with known light loads
Robot joints, machine tools with variable loads
blocks.caption: Choosing between stepper and servo positioning

blocks.markdown: **Gear ratio selection.** Motors are often fast with low torque, whereas machines need slow, strong motion. A gearbox with ratio $G$ (motor turns per output turn, $G>1$ for reduction) and efficiency $\eta$ trades speed for torque. Power is conserved apart from losses, so torque is multiplied by $G\eta$ and speed is divided by $G$.

blocks.caption: Gearbox with ratio G and efficiency eta

blocks.title: Choosing a gear ratio
blocks.prompt: A motor delivers 0.10 N m continuously and can run up to 3000 rpm. A mechanism needs 2.0 N m at 30 rpm. The gearbox efficiency is 0.80. Find the minimum ratio and check the speed.

steps.text: Pick a standard ratio 30:1 and check the output torque.
Motor speed needed to give 30 rpm at the output.

blocks.answer: A 30:1 gearbox supplies 2.4 N m at the output and needs only 900 rpm from the motor, so both torque and speed requirements are met with margin.

items: Higher microstepping gives finer motion and smoother running but does not increase accuracy or holding torque by the same factor.
Choose a motor whose pull-out torque exceeds the load with a margin (often 30 to 50 %).
Gear reduction multiplies torque and reduces speed, and also reduces the load inertia seen by the motor by $G^2$.
Backlash in a gearbox adds positioning error that an open-loop stepper cannot detect.

blocks.title: Do not trust open-loop where a stall is dangerous
blocks.text: If a lost step could cause a crash or injury (a gantry hitting its end stop, a clamp not closing), add feedback or a limit switch, or use a servo.

points: Step angle $=360^\circ/N_{rev}$; with microstepping $m$, steps for a rotation $=\Delta\theta/(\theta_s/m)$.
Stepper: open-loop, simple, can silently lose steps; servo: closed-loop, corrects errors, needs a sensor and tuning.
A gearbox gives $T_{out}=G\eta T_{motor}$ and $\omega_{out}=\omega_{motor}/G$; choose $G$ to meet the load torque and speed.

questions.stem: A stepper motor has a step angle of 7.5 degrees. How many full steps make one revolution?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: 24 corresponds to 15 degrees per step.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: 96 corresponds to 3.75 degrees per step.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this confuses the step angle with the step count.

questions.stem: What is the main risk of using an open-loop stepper motor for positioning?

options.text: The motor can skip steps under overload without the controller knowing
It cannot hold position at rest
It requires an encoder to run

questions.correctOptionText: The motor can skip steps under overload without the controller knowing

distractorRationale.a: Correct: with no feedback, lost steps are invisible.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: steppers have strong holding torque when energised.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: no sensor is required in open-loop operation.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: steppers are excellent at low-speed motion.

questions.explanation: Without feedback the controller assumes every commanded pulse became one step. If the load torque exceeds the pull-out torque the rotor misses steps and the recorded position becomes wrong.

questions.stem: A gearbox with a 10:1 reduction (ignoring losses) is placed between a motor and its load. What happens at the output shaft compared with the motor?

options.text: Speed is 10 times lower and torque is 10 times higher
Speed is 10 times higher and torque is 10 times lower
Both speed and torque are 10 times higher

questions.correctOptionText: Speed is 10 times lower and torque is 10 times higher

distractorRationale.a: Correct: power is conserved, so a speed reduction gives a proportional torque increase.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: this describes a 1:10 speed-increasing gearbox.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: that would multiply power by 100.

questions.explanation: For an ideal gearbox $T_{out}=GT_{motor}$ and $\omega_{out}=\omega_{motor}/G$ so the product (power) is unchanged.

questions.stem: A 1.8 degree stepper is driven with 1/8 microstepping. How many pulses are needed to rotate the shaft by 90 degrees?

distractorRationale.b: Wrong: 50 full steps would be needed without microstepping.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this doubles the correct count.

questions.explanation: The effective step is $1.8/8=0.225^\circ$, so $n=90/0.225=400$ pulses.

questions.stem: Which application is best served by an open-loop stepper rather than a closed-loop servo?

options.text: A light, fixed-load indexing table in a low-cost labelling machine
A robot joint whose load varies and must hold position against disturbance
A machine tool spindle axis cutting hard material
A gimbal that must correct for unpredictable vibration

questions.correctOptionText: A light, fixed-load indexing table in a low-cost labelling machine

distractorRationale.a: Correct: known light loads fit stepper open-loop control and save cost.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: variable loads risk lost steps; a servo corrects them.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: cutting forces vary and may exceed pull-out torque, so feedback is needed.

questions.explanation: Open-loop stepping is acceptable when the load torque is known, constant and well below the pull-out torque. Variable or disturbing loads need feedback.

questions.stem: A 1.8 degree stepper is driven with 1/16 microstepping and receives 275 pulses. Through what angle (in degrees) does the shaft turn?
A mechanism needs 1.5 N m. The motor provides 0.12 N m, and the gearbox efficiency is 0.85. What is the minimum gear reduction ratio?
questions.explanation: $G\ge T_{load}/(\eta T_{motor})=1.5/(0.85\times0.12)=14.7$. Choose the next standard ratio, such as 15:1 or 16:1.

questions.stem: A motor produces 0.090 N m at 4000 rpm and drives a load through a 40:1 gearbox of efficiency 0.90. What is the mechanical power at the output shaft, in watts?
questions.explanation: Motor power is $P=T\omega=0.090\times(4000\times2\pi/60)=37.7$ W. The output power is $0.90\times37.7=33.9$ W. The output torque is $40\times0.9\times0.09=3.24$ N m at 100 rpm, which gives the same 33.9 W.

questions.stem: Compare open-loop stepper and closed-loop servo positioning for a gantry that carries tools of varying mass and must never lose position. State which you would choose and why.
markingGuide: Stepper: open-loop, counts pulses, no feedback, cheaper and simpler
Stepper can skip steps if the load exceeds pull-out torque and the loss is undetected
Servo: encoder feedback compares actual with commanded position and corrects error
Servo maintains torque over a wider speed range and handles variable loads
Chooses servo (or a stepper with encoder feedback) for variable load and no-loss requirement, accepting higher cost
questions.explanation: A stepper counts pulses without feedback, which is simple and cheap but can silently lose steps if the varying tool mass pushes the torque beyond pull-out. A servo measures position and corrects any error, so it keeps accuracy under variable load at higher cost and with tuning effort. For a gantry that must not lose position, the servo is the better choice.

questions.stem: A 1.8 degree stepper at 1/4 microstepping drives a lead screw of 4.0 mm pitch directly. Calculate the number of pulses to move 25 mm, and the pulse frequency needed for a speed of 50 mm/s. State what limits how fast the pulse rate can be raised in practice.
markingGuide: Revolutions for 25 mm = 25/4 = 6.25, so pulses = 6.25 x 800 = 5000
Limit: pull-out torque falls with speed, so load torque and acceleration must stay within the motor's torque-speed curve or steps are lost
questions.explanation: There are $200\times4=800$ pulses per revolution, and 25 mm requires $25/4=6.25$ revolutions, so $6.25\times800=5000$ pulses. A speed of 50 mm/s is $12.5$ rev/s, requiring $12.5\times800=10{,}000$ pulses per second. In practice the available torque falls as speed rises, so the load and acceleration must stay inside the torque-speed curve or the motor will skip steps.
